claims.text: A conventional graphene-free W–Cu composite is used for heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications.
Monolayer or few-layer graphene can be integrated uniformly into the Cu phase of a W–Cu composite.
Graphene has intrinsically high thermal conductivity.
Graphene incorporated into the Cu phase will create additional high-thermal-conductivity pathways in W–Cu.
The graphene/Cu interface will reinforce the integrity of the Cu matrix.
Robust graphene–Cu interfacial bonding will maintain mechanical load transfer.
Robust graphene–Cu interfacial bonding will mitigate defect accumulation.
Adding a small, well-dispersed graphene fraction to the Cu phase will increase the effective thermal conductivity of W–Cu relative to graphene-free W–Cu.
The graphene-reinforced W–Cu composite will retain mechanical durability comparable to the graphene-free baseline.
The graphene-reinforced W–Cu composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to the graphene-free baseline.
The proposed benefits will hold under high heat flux, mechanical loading, and irradiation conditions typical of fusion reactors.
Uniform graphene dispersion and strong graphene–Cu interfacial bonding are necessary for the proposed benefits.
Excessive graphene content or poor dispersion may cause processing defects or interfacial problems.
Processing defects or interfacial problems caused by excessive or poorly dispersed graphene may degrade mechanical performance.
Ion implantation can simulate irradiation damage relevant to neutron exposure in this W–Cu system.
